utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and those assisting us outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I do understand that there are still some problems in respect of the tapes that are copied by now, the tapes provided by Mr. Gray. Is that correct? Or are the parties for the time being able to work as they should? If there are no observations in respect of that issue -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. What we said was the following, very briefly: Is that the originals are necessary to us, not just the copies. We simply wanted to know when we will be able to have the originals that we never really wanted to tender as such. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The originals will stay with the registry at this moment. We promised that they would be given back to Mr. Gray. At that time there had been no objections against that, so therefore the originals will stay with the registry at this moment with the promise that they would be given back to Mr. Gray at the time there had been no objection against that. So therefore, the originals will stay with the registry, the parties have been provided with copies. And if there's any need to compare at a certain issue copies and originals or to inspect the originals, you can apply to -- each party can apply to do that. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we'll have a problem, that we never wanted to tender the originals as such, only the sections that we viewed. We would like to be very clear on that point. We don't see why the originals, many more of them than all the sections we've shown, would be tendered. In our mind there's no reason for this to be tendered in totality. What was necessary is to have nine segments and that's all. And also, I gave my word, and I'd like to make sure that I stand by it, is that we would return that to Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Chamber gave its word as well to return it. We'll check it in the transcript, but it's my recollection -- it's the Chamber's recollection, because we briefly discussed the matter, but we'll check every detail, that the Chamber would take care of it after having copied the videos that they would be sent back to Mr. Gray. For the time being, they are available for inspection by the parties in order to see whether, especially if the copies would not be a -- would not be a copy that would be workable for the further preparation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wish to say was that the first versions that were copied and that I had, they didn't seem to be corresponding to the originals. But because I didn't have the originals, I couldn't compare. The images were a very poor quality. One would think that this was the cinema from the beginning of last century. I do not recall that this was the quality of the originals that were handed over. Now, if these tapes had deteriorated in quality during the copying procedure, I don't know. But we really have a problem here in terms of handling these videotapes, because this is something that was viewed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, first of all, I have been informed that a second copy, presumably a better copy, has been provided to you, so that you have, apart from the copy of, as you say, poor quality - the Chamber of course couldn't check that - but apart from that, you have a second copy now. If with -- on certain parts a few lines on it, if you'd like on these specific parts where the quality seems to be deficient, the original tapes are available for consultation, especially on these issues. The Chamber has, as far as my recollection goes - but if I'm wrong, we'll certainly check that - has promised to Mr. Gray that the Chamber is responsible for sending them back. The Chamber will do that. And finally, I do understand that you have only the same intent, that is, that the tapes are returned to Mr. Gray and that the content of the tapes is available for the parties, although not -- not tendered as a whole but only certain parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I raise something in relation to that or respond. There are two aspects to the relevance of the copying. The first -- and I should add the viewing by Mr. Gray. The first was that he was to identify, if he could, the part of the tapes which showed the crater in his evidence made by the bomb at the marketplace. The second point of relevance, especially the taping, was to establish where on the tapes disclosed to the Prosecution and provided by Mr. Gray were the two first segments shown by the Defence. I don't know in respect of the first whether Mr. Grey has indicated outside the Trial Chamber where on the tapes the crater appears. You may recall he said it was on the tape. Mr. President, we have received, I think on Friday, two video cassettes which appear to be copies made of the tapes provided. So I assume -- there are two further copies still coming. The two we have received -- excuse me. And we've now received the third one today. So I assume there's a fourth one coming. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is -- of the missing tape, there's a copy available for the Prosecution, since the originals are still in the hands of the registry. So that problem would have been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume that Mr. Gray has left the jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I assume as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I be informed as to whether he did indicate on any of the tapes the image of the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I am aware of, he did not. He did not review the tapes. That was partly due to the slow reproduction and the -- but I'll ask the registry to check with the Victims and Witnesses Unit whether he has reviewed the tape and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it has not been done. So if this would be vital information for you, Mr. Ierace, we'll have to seek another -- you'll have to seek another way to get to it. Then the parties, in order to avoid whatever confusion, the Chamber would prefer the parties to say exactly what they tender and on what tape it to be found. I take it since the originals will be sent back to Mr. Gray and we don't need them any more, it should be clear -- perhaps a short note would be the best way of dealing with it so that Madam Registrar has the guidance she needs. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on this issue, we're going to have a problem. Contrary to what the Prosecution has done - I may be mistaken, but I don't think this is the case, for once - the Defence handed over the entirety of the prepared segments, these nine segments that we viewed in the courtroom. That is not the case as far as the Prosecution is concerned because I think that they also prepared a summary of what they'd prepared. But we only have about two or three of the segments out of six or seven that were shown. So here we have a technical problem because the Defence will not accept that as an exhibit Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are tendered the segments that were neither seen by the witness nor by your Chamber. Now, that is a technical problem. I don't know what is to be done, only that the segments should be copied that were shown in the courtroom. I don't know how the Prosecution will handle this. That is a problem that I'm raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not to my understanding that the Prosecution wants to tender parts of the tape that have not been played or -- does it? No. So in that respect, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, none of the exhibits for the witness Richard Gray have yet been tendered. Could I respectfully suggest that we nominate a day later in the week to do that and prior to that date the Prosecution indicate now that they also have copies from which tape the first two segments were obtained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that your problem is where to find it on the tapes that have been disclosed to you now and that you do not intend to tender any part of the tape that has not been played in court. Then perhaps it would be good that the parties try to communicate in this respect so that we can deal with it in the most efficient way later this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the -- just for our clarification, does the Prosecution intend to tender specific parts of the tape not yet tendered by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is the parts which were shown during the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Of Richard Gray by the Prosecution. We have tendered, or at least Madam Registrar has a tape, of compilations from which we have played some segments. And you may recall that the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Indicated it didn't need to see any further segments. We don't rely on those. We don't tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it not be -- just for clarity sake, if you could copy the parts played on one tape so that the registry has no tape on which sequences do appear which are withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Alternatively, Mr. President, if we could have the tape back, we could wipe the sections that were not shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- at least if you have not then lengthy parts where nothing appears, because then people might think that that was the end of the tape, whereas after two, three, four, or five minutes a new part comes up. So that there's no clear order that should be written clearly on the tape in beginning or spots indicating so that there will be no confusion, no misunderstanding. Yes. If the parties would then continue to prepare, then we finally will deal with the matter later this week. Then I have to inform the parties that we had a late start because of the other hearing this morning, because the other hearing this morning took more time and was finished late. Is the -- is there any need to re-examine Dr. Vilicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please, Madam Usher, could you please escort Professor Vilicic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Professor Vilicic. Welcome back in the courtroom. We had a late start, and we had some procedural issues to deal with as well. So, therefore, you had to wait for a while. Our apologies for that. You'll now be further examined by counsel for the Defence. May I remind you, as I did before several times, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are now going to go back to your first day of cross-examination by the Prosecution. That was the 26th of February. You were asked a question by the Prosecution in relation to the state of one of the craters on the site of the Dobrinja parking in relation to the football match incident, and you started answering this question speaking of red paint. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us, Professor, what did you mean to say by this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I was told by Stamatovic that these traces, or rather, that the crater on the asphalt had been filled by red paint, that in a way they had been protected by further damage. These sites were protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. Am I to understand your answer that in a sense the crater had been filled up again, had been closed?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What they did, they kept practically the outside view of the crater but you couldn't measure the depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, Professor, except if you could reopen that crater, there was nothing else that you could have used, any other element, except this external appearance of the crater. Is that correct; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Objectively it's not interesting because the angle of descent of the projectile, we would consider the frontal swathe of the shell and the only question was the depth. But bearing in mind the appearance, it was obvious that the depth could not have been any other than the depth that we took from the report of the security centre and the forensic experts that measured it and examined it on the site of the incident at the time when the crater still existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, let us now talk about front lines. You were subject to a series of questions in relation to the positions of the front lines, and you were given documents by the Prosecution, and these documents were referring to the Serb version of your text, of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know where these documents are now. I believe they are in the hands of Madam Registrar, unless they were returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are you referring to the filed report in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, I'm speaking of three exhibits that don't yet have numbers, but they are referring to the Serb version of the text of the report. I have that here, if this is of any assistance. These three maps. Thank you, Madam Registrar. These three maps, could they please be placed again before the expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we will start by the map bearing the number 34, page number 34. And I would be very grateful if you can tell us whether the line as it has been positioned on the left-hand side, that is, to the west, whether this line corresponds or not to what you finally kept in the English text.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It doesn't correspond. But let me say: With the Serb version - because we thought that the English version was needed by the Court - we also appended also the corrections of the four pages. These were corrections for pages 25, 26. I think it was also for page 43. But -- sorry, no, it was 34 and also -- and for 43, yes. These four pages, we've attached the corrections primarily because of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to interrupt you. My question - and could you please focus on the questions - is very simply the following: Could you please take page 34 that you were just handed. Very well. Now, could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you please compare it with page 34 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I to put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no, no. There's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, just this line here, just this line, the one this way, now it's going this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, please, listen to my question and answer when I finish my question. Is there - yes or no - in relation to the English text, that is, page 34, as it was tendered, the English text, is there a difference - yes or no - between the confrontation lines in the west?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old version doesn't, but the new documents that were tendered, they do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please place the -- what you call the old version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. In the English version, in the English version -- I checked. No, it's mistaken. There's no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, for future reference, can you please listen to the questions carefully and answer. So there's no difference. Thank you very much. Now, Professor, let us take the map that you were just handed, and the page number is 47, please. No, the one that you were just handed -- Professor. Professor, the page -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you see this document before you? Can you please put it on the ELMO with the assistance of Madam Usher. Professor, the line to the west, the one that's circled, does it have any effect on any conclusion that one would be able to draw in relation to the direction of fire, which seems to come more from the east than from the west?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On what basis, my learned friend, speaking about the direction of fire which seems to come more from the east?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if that arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the objection is -- or at least the question is whether what the factual basis is that the fire seems to come more from the east than from the west. Are we talking about a specific incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I'm going to repeat. On the basis of the compass points. There is north, south, east, and west. There is a key, which is very clear for everyone to see. For instance, the origin of fire is marked with an arrow. It goes from right to left. And as far as I'm concerned, this comes more from the east than from the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still speaking about the map. Is the objection sustained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... is the arrow on this map. The objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, Professor, you were unfortunately interrupted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me just -- if you want to ask the witness - I think that's what you did - whether the difference in confrontation lines would make any difference to the arrow of the source of fire from the east, I mean whatever he says, I think the Chamber is well aware that if you fire at a distance of less than 40.000 kilometres, if the fire comes from the east, a confrontation line that the west could have some influence on, from which side of the confrontation line it comes. So it's not really necessary to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But we waste a lot of time on these maps. And this stems from the Prosecution questions. That's why I wanted to proceed in this way. But if everything is clear for the Chamber, all the better. And then we no longer have to talk about the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, let us now go to the problem of the car -- of the water queue incident and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be kind enough to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the interpreters are having difficulties in hearing and translating your question. They asked to repeat it. They asked that in English. So would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was listening to the Serb booth. Which one is having difficulties, the Serb booth or the English booth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We'll start again. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall there was a picture of a motor vehicle, of a car, and this was taken in sine cosine in a way, it was reversed, so that you would make it more adapted to your position as an expert, so that you can view it better. My question is the following: First of all, do you recall that, Professor; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do. And I explained. It was 180 degrees reversal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. Thank you. My question is the following: Was there in anything that the position of this photograph, that is, as it appears either in negative or in positive, would it have changed your conclusions in relation to this incident; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you. Professor, I would like to now go back to the football match incident. You were questioned at length about the difference of altitude, a difference in the altitude of the terrain. And it was said that around this area there was an elevated position, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. It was about effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Exactly. My question is as follows: When one examines the distance between the impact point and the position where these spectators were allegedly located, the fact that they were slight -- at a slightly more elevated position, perhaps standing, perhaps sitting down in some cases, would this have changed anything? Would this have made a difference with regard to the dispersal of the fragments and as a result with regard to the statistical results that concern the victims?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had -- I said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... but when the question is phrased in terms of "slightly," that is too vague. The question ought to be framed in a more precise manner, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the -- it's clear from the witness what has been put to the witness during cross-examination, that we're talking about people that are -- might have been 2 or 3 metres higher -- slightly higher, or on cars, which is also some, I would say, 1 metre 60 up to 2 and a half metres. If that is the understanding of all the parties, it would be my understanding. And I take it, Professor Vilicic, that you understood the question also in a similar way. So on the basis of that, would that have altered your conclusion -- your conclusions and calculations as far as the dispersion is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in the course of the examination-in-chief, all the spectators were in this area, in this rectangle on page 32, this rectangle which surrounds this area. They were far closer than they would have been -- or some of them were far closer, and that's unfavourable as far as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the number of those hit is concerned. They were far closer than if we had taken them to be these elevations which were further away and the effect of the projectile wouldn't have been as great in that case and there wouldn't have been as many hurt. So we took the most unfavourable position. If they had all been close to the point of impact, near the area where the game was held, in that case the projectile would have had -- would have been most effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. I'd like you to be shown an exhibit which is a triple x-ray, it seems. It's an x-ray of the explosion of a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Madam Registrar, it's this image. It's this image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a shell. It's an artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I -- in French I said "a shell," "mortar shell." I don't know who said "artillery shell."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the English booth, I didn't mention a mortar shell. I mentioned a shell.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you saw these shells, do you remember that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The picture, yes, I saw it. Mr. Stamp asked questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You were asked questions, Professor, about the swelling of the fuse. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, you were asked questions about the type of material used for this part, or rather, you were asked what metal was used, and you answered the question - do you remember that - for this type of shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember mentioning metal. I mentioned the difference in the thickness of the case, of the projectile case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, on page 52 you said that -- with regard to that zone, that part, you said that it was an aluminium part. It's not in your report. It's in the transcript. Do you remember that? We're talking about the extreme part of the detonator.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, with regard to an artillery shell, I couldn't have mentioned an aluminium part. When I analysed this picture, I said it didn't correspond to the way in which a mortar shell explodes, given that it has thinner walls. I was asked whether the case swelled. I said it did. And when it swells, the case is opened and the fuse or part of the fuse is ejected. And then Mr. Stamp asked me whether I agreed that part of the fuse could also be deformed, and I said that it was possible, that they could be deformed, but it depended on the fuse, the kind of fuse used. If it's a UTM 78 fuse, the dimensions of which are quite big, then there's enough room for part of the fuse which is made of aluminium to also be deformed. For UTM-68 [as interpreted], there's no possibility for the fuse to become deformed because the diameter is 25.4 millimetres smaller. It is more likely that it will be ejected and it will be broken. There are no elements that could be -- that could swell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. In order to make sure that everything is clear. You suggested to examine two photographs -- I suggested you examine two photographs and in relation to these photographs, you said that with regard to a grenade -- a mortar shell, we're talking about mortar shells now, you said that with such a weapon, such ammunition, there were no aluminium parts. Can you confirm that? Bearing in mind the answer you provided with regard to this type of shell.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, Professor. It seems that according to the preceding transcript, you mentioned that a constituent part of these artillery shells was an aluminium part, and you asked about this. What I want to know is whether you stand by what you stated with regard to mortar shells. And you said that such mortar shells didn't have any aluminium parts. And I'm now talking about mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about a 120-millimetre mortar shell, the only aluminium parts are parts of the fuse. And the body of the shell, the stabiliser, are made of steel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I might need the assistance -- well, probably, yes, I think I'll need the assistance of a technician because I wanted to cover a lot of things but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I think I'd like to address the question of penetration, with regard to the stabilisers. You were asked a certain number of questions as to whether the first explosion in a certain sense opened the way or made it possible for the stabiliser to penetrate the ground after the explosion. My question is: The firing tables that you mentioned, do they take into consideration such factors? For example, we're talking about table 8 here.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the action of the fuse. If it's an instantaneous fuse, the shell will explode and the shell won't penetrate very far. If it is a delayed action fuse, then the shell shall penetrate the ground to a greater extent. So with regard to your question, the stabiliser will penetrate further if you use a time delay shell, since the shell creates a bigger crater. If it explodes on the surface, then -- I mean, if it's instantaneous, if the fuse is a super-quick fuse, then the crater will be smaller and as a result it will be more difficult for the stabiliser to penetrate further. Let's put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. But my question was: The firing tables that you used -- not the firing tables. The tables that you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The tables that you used, table 8 in particular, do these tables take into consideration the -- the formulas that are included in these tables, do they take into consideration the fact that an explosion takes place before the penetration of the stabiliser? This is my question. That is to say, is the fact that -- is the fact that some of the ground is blown out, ejected, is that taken into consideration in the tables themselves?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think your question is -- well, I'll answer like this: Table 8 or table 7, both of them, take into consideration that the time of reaction of the fuse is 1 millisecond. During that 1 millisecond, the projectile passes a trajectory that we can call LPR. After 1 millisecond, for the sake of an example, a mortar shell in the first column, 46 degrees, at a speed of 67 metres -- well, if the fuse didn't activate, it would only cover a trajectory of 18 centimetres. But since the fuse activated after 1 millisecond, then the shell explodes only after it has penetrated 6 centimetres into the ground. And these are the calculations. This is a fact that we used in all our analysis, in all the five cases which concerned mortar shells and the depth of -- where the depth of penetration had been recorded. So table 7 or table 8 have to do with crater depth for projectiles which functioned properly, if they exploded normally and if the fuse was instantaneous, if it was activated after 1 millisecond. If you reduce this time, this reaction time, then the penetration depth would be smaller because the more the time is reduced, the less the depth of penetration. The more time it takes for the fuse to activate, the further it penetrates. So if the fuse is quick, the quicker it is, the faster the fuse acts, the more the penetration depth will be reduced. It's faster if this value is lower than 1. One is 1 millisecond. If it were 0.5, that would be -- .5 milliseconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But first I would like to ask, Mr. President, a question concerning the break. Is it going to be at quarter to or later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'll have our first break a bit later because we started a quarter of an hour later. I intend to have the first break at approximately 4.00. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we'll move on to another subject. I would like you to take the English version of the report that you provided us with and have a look at page 28, please. Just a minute. But if we have a look at page 42, you were referred to the existence of three projectiles in your report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is: Would you like to comment on why, although you mentioned three impacts, only two are referred to in your map and something in regard -- in relation to the position of these impact points? Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here, according to the record of the ballistics expert, three impact points were recorded, three points of impact that had been hit by projectiles. Two were ascribed to an 82-millimetre mortar. And on a soil surface, on the appearance of the crater, the destruction caused, one could come to the conclusion that the shell used was a 120-millimetre shell. So in that picture there, the first and third projectile were mortar shells, were 82-millimetre mortar shells, and the third projectile, which overflew the building and fell on this soil surface, penetrated to a depth of 40 centimetres, it made a crater which was 40 centimetres deep. And that shell was a 120-millimetre shell. And as far as I can remember - I have the image here - that is a projectile that penetrated -- yes, it's -- image 268 -- 248, and the projectile penetrated at a degree of almost 90 degrees, an angle of almost 90 degrees. And you can see the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question, professor, had to do above all with what you said about the three projectiles and the figure, the plan, where these two projectiles are referred to, and in particular with regard to the question that was put to you, that is to say, whether the projectiles exploded or not in the courtyard of the building. And I wanted you, if you think this might be useful, to comment something about this matter. And they would certainly be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that the bodies of the stabilisers of the 82-millimetre shells weren't found, so we concluded that there was not precise evidence that 82-millimetre shells were used. But according to the appearance of the crater, one impact was on the edge - this is photograph 268-189 - according to the appearance of a crater the depth of penetration, on that basis we concluded that the shell used was probably an 82-millimetre shell. On the basis of the traces that we recorded, we came to the conclusion that that shell fell at a great drop angle because we made these calculations on the basis of the depth of the crater which was 6 centimetres and the ellipse which was formed during the explosion. These dimensions were provided in the report. And on that basis we came to the conclusion that the drop velocity was greater than 68 millimetres, greater than when just one main charge is used, and we came to the conclusion that one charge was used, and on the basis of the drop velocity used when you have one charge, the penetration depth corresponds to the values that we established at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for these answer, but my question had to do with the plan, quite simply. If there are any comments you could make about the plan that you made and the comments of the accusation about the shells that fell in the courtyard of the building, it would be a good time to make such comments. If not, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat this. I've said this on several occasions already. To analyse all these events, the appearance of the crater and the dimension of the crater was of primary importance to us. It was not relevant whether it was in front or behind a building. That wasn't interesting to us. Only if the building perhaps formed an obstacle to the projectile, that would have been interesting. But in this case, this was not relevant. It was primarily on the basis of the traces found on the site that we determined the parameters that could, let's say, reproduce such an event. We took into consideration the ellipse, the depth of penetration, et cetera, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We can take this off the ELMO, this document. And now, Mr. President, we would like to have a look at the figure that you sketched at the end of last week, and that is the cross-section of a mountainous position.

utterances.text: Professor, do you remember this sketch?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. Yes, I do. Yes. Yes, Mr. President, I made this sketch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The question that I wanted to ask was, first of all: What is the drop velocity, maximum drop velocity of a body that is launched in this way bearing in mind the air resistance? So what is the maximum speed while there would be no more acceleration?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends. If we are talking about free fall -- if we are talking about free fall, then we know that the acceleration of the earth's gravity has to be added to the velocity without resistance by extrapolating. That's how I got these results. So I was not able to get precisely the air resistance during the projectile movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, my question is the following -- my question is the following: Is there a point whether -- from which point there is a free fall of an object where it no longer accelerates, in terms of experiments that were made by dropping two balls and watching when and how they fall, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both balls will have the acceleration. The acceleration stops at the moment when the inertia of the body is zero, that is, when it stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. In general, in terms of artillery, what is the speed of the fall of an object in free fall when there is no more -- any acceleration that is influenced by gravity, when we come to zero point?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we equalise the resistance of the object which is going, then there's no more acceleration, so it is dropping at that rate. But in this case, it doesn't happen. We always have acceleration up to the moment of impact. I am talking about the situation presented on this sketch. What we have to know is that the firing tables were produced for an altitude of zero and for a flat surface. But if you have a situation of firing at a target which is higher than the firing point, that is, when you're firing at a target -- or if you're firing at a target which is lower than the firing position of the weapon, then it is normal that you have the so-called straightening of the trajectory because you move the position, you change the position, then the gravity -- the force of gravity will have a influence on a different angle in relation to the normal trajectory, the way it is calculated. So what will happen is that there will be a straightening of the trajectory and figuratively speaking, we will get a higher or longer range if we are firing at the same angle bearing in mind the distance from this point to this point, if we are talking about a topographic distance. If we take a topographic distance between the firing position and the drop point, the impact point that we wish to fire at, the target, in this case if the target is higher or lower than horizon of the weapon, then it would fire over the target. In other words, what you have to do is to carry out a correction of the firing. That will be the local angle of the target. It could be in positive or negative. And when firing is prepared, then you always have to carry out a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I don't know whether this is possible, but is it possible -- first of all, can you tell us what is an azimuth.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azimuth? Azimuth is the direction of firing toward which the weapon is positioned. Azimuth is the direction. That is the angle in relation to the north, which is the direction of the weapon, or in relation to -- in relation to north or in relation to some other chosen point according to which the firing is assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, if we look at the horizon, which will be the zero altitude point, is it possible if I want to hit a target lower down, if I'm working on the situation of an imaginary horizon, would it be the point of target? That is, if I modify my angle and my azimuth, therefore. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand. The azimuth is not in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I withdraw the azimuth. I withdraw the azimuth. Did you understand my question, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you mean -- if it is necessary to correct what I said, what happens if you have the target above or under -- I'm just looking to show you the graphic appearance of the trajectory of 120 high explosive mine -- a shell. Now, if the target is below the horizon, as it is shown on this sketch -- may I put this on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Piletta-Zanin does not oppose against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Things will be clearer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to me the question is not quite clear. What is clear to me is that the witness has already testified that if the target is higher, lower, or higher than the point of firing, the level of firing, that you would need to adjust your target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, please, could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain very briefly. Here. This line here, that is the zero line, the nought line. This is the line based on which the firing tables are done. This is nought line. In this case, the weapons go from nought and the target impacts, target sites are on this line. Now, these are the trajectories of the increment charges. Sixth, fifth, fourth, third, second, first. Specifically speaking, say that I'm using third increment charge. The projectile will fall on the target on this site, on this position. However, if the target is 500 metres below, then this projectile under the same angle of firing will fall here. That means it will go over the target. So, for instance, if this is about 3.900 metres, it will go at 500 metres. It will fall at the end of this trajectory. That will be roughly 4.250 to 4.300. What happens is that there is -- it will be firing over the target. Because of that, a correction has to be made. The same thing happens, is that if the target is, let us say, at the same distance but above and we are using third increment charge, then what I will get, if you draw a line up at 3.000 metres, for example sake we can take this point that I had initially taken, about 3.900 metres, and if at this point this target is up here, up here where I'm pointing now, then I would have to make a correction because of the change of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you see these lines here? These lines here are the lines of the local angle of the target, and that's why graphically we have to correct the firing, because if the target as at 500 metres - and I'm using the elements that I wanted to hit, the target at 3.900 - I will get the hit here. Here, you see. And perhaps I wanted to fire at the target 3.900. So what I have to do, is I have to rotate the curve, the trajectory. I have to seek an angle because I cannot use the third increment charge, but I'd have to use a different charge that will cover Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this point. So if I could have used the third increment charge, perhaps here I cannot use it there. I'll have to use the fifth or sixth increment charge to be able to hit the target that I had intended, because contrary to a straight line in small arms -- small weapons, these trajectories in here, they are curved trajectories and there are very large margins of error. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please keep in control of the examination. I mean, the witness has now used 30, 40, 50 lines in order to explain that an adjustment is needed. And of course that's the charge, that's the angle. This is, I would say, for every -- it's not really something that is in need of further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was on the point of interrupting the witness. But thank you very much for your assistance. This subject, I believe that this is a perfect moment for a break. And with your leave, perhaps we could finish very briefly when we reconvene.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have very few things. This is to do with acceleration and the differences between 500, 400, and so on, when we are firing at lower targets.

utterances.text: Yes. Shall we say 15 minutes, if I listen to what -- and then I take it that you'll --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Including the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, earlier you told us in relation to the table that you explained to us, which was on the ELMO, that when you are trying to hit a target which is lower than the nought position of the horizon, there are corrections that should be made so to speak. Now, my question is the following: If we examine such a situation where hypothetically speaking there would be firing from an altitude of over 300 metres from the distance from the target, what would be the probability of hitting the target the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On this issue, the probability of hitting, it is my submission that it did not arise in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But this is exactly the continuation of what the witness was explaining, because he spoke about corrections. Now, I know that the witness developed -- perhaps we could just let him develop briefly just on this matter, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the -- I expressed already that the explanation was not of great assistance because it was -- it wasn't subjected, it did not need much explanation. utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I read the transcript and the expert report of the professor, and the Defence believes that it is important for the public that certain things be explained because the public, they do not read expert reports every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, witness. Let us change the subject. utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. I gave the possible acceleration with the changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Professor. Thank you. My question is simply the following: Would there be a large difference or not - I don't know - in your calculations if we examined a difference of 400 metres in relation to a 500-metre difference?

utterances.text: Well, approximately, as I said, with the lowering of the altitude by 100 metres, for the highest charge the velocity changes by 4 metres per second. So basically for 400 metres you can say that there would be a 4 metre a second difference, if the weapon is 100 metres higher than the target it would be about 4 metres per second difference in speed, but depending on the data for calculating the trajectory, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very last question: In relation to the methods that you used and in relation to any comments that you could make with respect to what was found by the studies, the examinations, that were conducted in Sarajevo before you -- that is, did you know the results of such and such an expert, for instance, Mr. Zecevic, and such and such an institute in Sarajevo, and my question in relation to this is: What can you tell us about the methodologies that were used and also of the necessity in this case to establish commissions or committees that would be of an international nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, this doesn't arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it does, Mr. President, because on several occasions the Prosecution, unless they have something else to say -- the Prosecution asked the professor certain questions on the conclusions reached by such and such a commission, in relation to such and such an incident. So I believe that it would be good for the professor if he thinks he can, what he was able to observe on terms of methodology and in relation to his own experience, if he could explain this to your Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No questions were asked in relation to the methodology. All that was inquired into was whether or not conclusions were consistent with his. And second, I don't think the professor is competent to testify about the international nature of committees and what the law requires or what practice requires. That's far outside of his competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. It does not arise from cross-examination, apart from the matter that it's not in the specific expertise of this -- of this expert, the methodology of setting up committees. Apart from that, the methodology of setting up is only of relative relevance. That was your last question, then Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Mr. Stamp, is there any need to -- no, it's now for the Judges. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench will put some questions to you as well, Professor Vilicic. It's first Judge Nieto-Navia who will put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like you to have a look on your table 12, page 56 of the English version. My question is whether this table is based on the Sandian or on the Berezin formulas.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it isn't. This is a form this table, table 13, on page 57. That's the probability, the hit probability for the Markale market if a 120-millimetre mortar shell is used. It's page 57. It's the hit probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... not 13, but 12.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Table 12 was done on the basis of the Sandia National Laboratory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: May I take it that in most of the tables we have used during your testimony the X of the equation is the depth of the penetration of the shell, and here in this table is a velocity, isn't it? I mean, the velocity is the result of this calculation in this table.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, LP is the depth of penetration, and VC is the impact of velocity. The impact of velocity of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I know that. But the penetration is linear, let's say. The velocity is not linear. So I take it that the velocity is the result of the application of the equation in this table.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look on your report, page 49. You are quoting some testimony, Witness number 2 says that "The shell could be seen over flying." Witness number 3: "I saw an object approaching," and so on. My question is whether it is possible to see a mortar shell when flying.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can only see a mortar shell if you are at the firing position, next to the weapon that means. And when the shot is fired, you can notice it if the velocity is up to about 300 metres. But if you are somewhere on the side, if you are in the direction where it's coming from, you can't see the shell. That is to say, if the shell is heading in your direction, in such cases you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, I have another issue here: You described in your report a theoretical model for predicting the number of victims due to mortar shells. Are there other models than the one you describe in your report which can be used to make such predictions?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The method that we used is the so-called method for checking the effectiveness of the projectile in an arena. And as far as we know, it's used in a number of European countries. It's a method which is a Western European method. For example, in France, probably in America too, we -- I haven't had the occasion to observe this but it's a method to use -- which is used to examine the effectiveness of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I'm sorry with the interpreters. Are you aware of other methods, different ones?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are simpler methods, yes. The older methods weren't so sophisticated. This model could be realised and developed thanks to the development of technology, computers, et cetera, and differential equations, et cetera. You can use this to make calculations and in a fairly short period of time you get reliable data. But the method was developed, an identical one in France. You check the efficiency of the projectile and of mortar shells. Information on fragments, the dispersal, velocity of the fragments, et cetera, we call this the lethal or effective action of the projectile. Unfortunately, against manpower this is tested in an arena and for each type of projectile it is determined when the projectile is being developed. Now, the quality of the -- the quantity of the explosives and the quantity of material used influences this. This is one of the basic procedures used in order to determine the nature of a shell made of a certain shell in order to determine how efficient it is, with regard to other types of projectiles. As an example, an 82-millimetre shell made in Yugoslavia. There were older ones -- there were older. This report also mentions more recent ones consisted of a mixture of TNT and hexogen in order to increase the velocity and in order to increase the lethal nature of the fragments, because in such case it is velocity is greater, they have a greater range, and the number of victims is greater. They cause more lethal wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: If I understand you well, this is a model method. There are other methods but not as model, as accurate as this one.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have the same question regarding the probability of hitting given target by firing a small number of shells. Are there other methods --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, that's the standard method which is used all over the world. These are statistical methods, and they depend on the -- well, depending on the statistical methods used, you know, there are several laws. There are laws on the division, and this is how these values are determined. It has to do with dispersals that are mentioned in firing tables and the values, the precision of hitting the target depends on these values. You have VD in the tables. It has dispersal for each projectile. And you have a greater possibility of hitting the target if that value is greater, the probability is less. You're not as likely to hit the target with one projectile. If you have a look at table 13, you will see that when you increase the distance, the firing range from the first to the sixth increment charge, as you increase it the probability of hitting the target with one projectile drops because VX [as interpreted], the possibility dispersal over a distance, this increases with the range. So, for example, in the case of the 36 metres of depth of the market for the first charge, it's 12 metres, so the projectile has to be incorrect on three occasions. And here was one mistake, if you use the sixth increment charge, it can hit an area outside of the market or it can hit the market itself. You understand. I think you understand me, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because since VD has a large value, there is greater dispersion. In such cases the possibility of hitting the target is less. So this is value 226 if I want to hit the market and if I want to be 100 per cent sure that I will hit the target, that I will achieve such a result, then in this last column, according to the laws of probability, in the first case or the first charge -- with one charge, you would need 11 projectiles in order for the projectiles to have a 90 per cent possibility of hitting that area. Then if you use 6 charges you need to fire 131 projectiles in order to have the same probability of hitting the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm going to another subject. As far as I understand Dr. Zecevic's report, he concluded that the shell landed at Markale had been fired from a distance in excess of 4 kilometres, as far as I remember. He reached this conclusion on a research which was published in the late 1990s regarding the minimum speed necessary for a mortar shell to lodge itself in the ground after an explosion. He then computed the minimum drop speed of the shell to deduce the number of charges which that shell carried and to determine the distance at which the shell had to have been fired. Assuming that a 120-millimetre mortar shell exploded at Markale and had a drop angle of between 55 and 65 degrees, could you give me or give to the Chamber an opinion on the reasoning that allowed Dr. Zecevic to conclude that the mortar had been fired from a distance in excess of 4 kilometres? I don't know whether I have been clear in my question. What I want you is to comment on the reasoning of Dr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, Your Honour, I followed Professor Zecevic's testimony before this Trial Chamber and the first thing that was said was that the stabiliser wasn't present, that when he placed the stabiliser in the hole, by using a protractor he measured that the angle of the fins was between 20 and 30 degrees. I followed the text and I made a note - I think so it was on page 25, line 8 to 11, something like that - and I also noticed that the kiosk which was hit on the edge was mentioned and it was determined that there was an angle of 50 degrees between the edge of the kiosk and the impact point. I don't know how he could have come to the conclusion that the speed was 60 metres -- that a speed of 60 metres was sufficient for the projectile to penetrate to the extent that it did. All our calculations show that this is not possible. If I return to the first fact that an angle of 20 to 30 degrees was established at the very beginning, that was an angle -- a drop angle of 60 to 70 degrees. If you take -- you obtain this result for the drop angle. And later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I'm sorry. My question is the following: As far as I understand the reasoning of Professor Zecevic, he calculated the minimum speed necessary for the shell to penetrate a certain amount of centimetres in the ground, and then he deduced the number of charges used to reach that velocity. My question is: Do you agree or you don't agree with this methodology?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree because the results that he obtained, that he presented - and on page 27 he said that on the basis of the Sutterlin method, he said that he established that 60 metres wasn't a sufficient speed for the stabiliser to penetrate to a depth of 260 millimetres. This does not correspond to the Sutterlin method. You don't obtain these results on the basis of this method nor on the basis of the Berezin method. And that's why we came to the conclusion that this was not possible. We concluded that in such conditions that the stabiliser could not penetrate in this way, because from a distance of 4.000 metres he said that a velocity of 200 metres was sufficient, if you take away 140 then the relative velocity that the stabiliser has, 60 metres, it's enough to penetrate to a depth of 260 millimetres. So that's what I've noted in my papers here and that was in the testimony that I followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor. The UN expert concluded that it was impossible to determine with a reasonable degree of accuracy the drop angle of the shell because the recovered tail fin had been extracted from the ground. But in your report, on pages 50 to 153, you provide some trigonometric calculations to determine the drop angle of the shell. I'm talking of Markale. And you determined that based on the imprints left by the explosion -- I think that this is the same methodology used by Professor Zecevic. Are you confident of this computed drop angle or the value provided by you is just a, let's say, technical or educated guess given the circumstances of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 53, our conclusion is that on the basis of the values measured, the measurements which we found in Zecevic's report and in the forensic ballistics report, the parameters 56 and 26 are the measurements for the ellipse. And we determined that the drop angle with the first charge could be 56 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the figures and could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Please, please the interpreters cannot follow you. Will you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 53, on the basis of the parameters which were measured at the Markale market -- that's A value, that's the fourth item. That's 56 centimetres and B is 26 centimetres, on that basis we determined that the drop angle could be 62.5 degrees, if you're using one increment charge, and 55.6 degrees if you're using a sixth increment charge. In other words, as I have already said, we confirmed that the drop angle on the basis of these parameters could be between 55 and 65 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to be sure that I have understood you correctly. Let's start with what you stated. You stated that the fragments -- the shell fragments, when the shell explodes, you don't calculate the fragments that go beyond 2 metres, taking into account the fact that beyond 2 metres you no longer hit the normal figure -- have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question from the Defence today, you were asked whether the fact that the spectators at the football match - and some of them, it seems, were at elevated points, on cars, et cetera - you said that that did not affect your conclusions in any way. Your conclusions, which were based, if I have understood you correctly, on the fact that you did not include fragments that went beyond 2 metres. And the conclusion was that if the spectators were sitting or standing but were at a distance exceeding 2 metres but were within the range of the explosion, they could have been hit.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that we thought -- we took all the spectators to be on the playground. So these conditions are far more severe with regard to the probability of hitting people, in relation to those who were further away and in relation to those who were at elevated positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Professor. My second question concerns the existence of aluminium in the shells, the issue of whether this material existed in the shells or not. If I have understood your testimony, you said that the fuse was surrounded by aluminium. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the fuse is a dead weight, so to speak. So one tries to make it as light as possible in order to have as much explosives and steel as possible in the projectile. The fuse is an additional element. It's not the key part. It has not got any key importance for the functioning of the projectile, the effectiveness of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you speak about a shell that you called M-78? Is this general knowledge? Is this a matter of general knowledge that Serbia produced shells -- M-78 shells? Are these the same shells, do they have the same characteristics?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An M-78 fuse is produced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't want to interrupt, but I thought that in the language used by Judge El Mahdi M-78 -- 77, and in the transcript, and in the translation it says "M-78." So my question has to do with the transcript, which is not quite exact, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness understood the question quite well, and he was answering the question. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. M-78 fuse was produced in the former Yugoslavia. The main producer of fuses was in a factory in Bugojno, the Slavko Rodic factory. But this was in Krusik Valjevo. This fuse was also made in Krusik Valjevo in Serbia now. And for 82-millimetre shells which are produced by Krusik Valjevo you have modern fuses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was talking about 120-millimetre shells but of 77 -- of 77 shells. I'm talking to you as a layman and on the basis of general knowledge. The M-77 model isn't produced in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 77?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what projectile an M-77 is, a 120-millimetre one. We don't have such a projectile. Our projectiles are 120-millimetre projectiles, instantaneous ones. The 56 model I think it's designated as P1 and the 120-millimetre ones, the fuse can be of various kinds. You can have UTUM 62, it can be UTUM 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir, you say you are not familiar with the projectile ATN 77 produced in Serbia. Very well. Your answer is no; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with such a projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If you don't mind, I'd like to move on to another subject. On page 56 of the English version of your report, after the table, you say: [In English] "There is no mortar of such ballistics." [Interpretation] Are you following me? It's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: I think that you came to your conclusions on the basis of the various methods in existence, the various methods for measuring, which are based on, if I may call it like this, military functioning. The tables that you used, their purpose was to test the effectiveness and the means of defence -- both of the means of defence and -- well, isn't that correct? You were asked some questions about the terrain. It was said that there was a 2-centimetre layer of asphalt, and then that there was stones, small stones. I think I understood that the results were not effective as such in order to come to the conclusion that you provided by basing yourself on research which had a military interest, which was a military nature and was carried out in other fields and its purpose was different, it was to be applied in different ways. That is to say, given the nature of the ground, do you stand by the conclusions you reached to the extent that you yourself -- in that you yourself said that the results obtained were calculated by taking into consideration a layer which was greater, a layer of hard material that was greater?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've explained it to here and having looked at all the additional tables, apart from what is already in the expert report, this gave us the results to conclude that 120-millimetre mortar shell under that angle, the drop velocity that it has cannot give such a result in terms of depth of penetration. Another conclusion was that a mortar shell was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I apologise. Let us pass by the question of the angle, this angle or a different angle.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The angle here is just a reference value given here for our conclusion that we reached. This is based on a multifaceted assessment, on the calculation measurements for the depth of penetration, and they didn't show that this was possible, also the calculation of an effectiveness of a 120-millimetre mortar shell, and also considering our experience in this, so that had it not been an accident, if somebody with 120-millimetre mortar, if that person had hit this Markale target at such a distance that would have been somebody who would need a prize. Now, what we've checked for 120-millimetre mortar shells made in Yugoslavia, they do not have such effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, effectiveness, do you mean firing precision? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. What I mean is the effectiveness -- effectiveness of the projectile itself, the number of people who were hit on a given area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's another thing. My first question was the possibility or impossibility for a shell gets to that depth and the stabiliser becomes embedded in the soil. You said that that would necessitate a velocity that is impossible, that doesn't exist, that is not known, and you rule out categorically the possibility that the incident could have occurred in the way that it was described. And my question was in relation to your conclusion. Your conclusion is multilayered, in the sense that you have used methods that were for military objectives for hitting shelter targets rather than a surface which consisted of a relatively thin asphalt-layered surface and then of stone. Now, do you understand what I mean by this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it, but we used those coefficients - and that's why we've used several methods - we used the Berezansky's formula as a base and the Sandian laboratory formula that we used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Berezansky's for instance is adapted but however, you've added an element which was a subjective element, that is such -- you did not apply one specific method. You've modified the result according to your assessment. And on the basis of what? On the basis of what did you make this difference, did you make this change?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Berezansky, Sandia, and Gabeaud methods, we didn't modify them. We only used the coefficients and the data that are given officially. Here I have original copies of Gabeaud, Berezansky formula I also have, and the coefficient for such surfaces. What was contested here was the Sandian laboratory method. In my answers I was not really ready to answer that. I was not prepared that there would be discussion about details. In the meantime I have this report. I read it, and my conclusion is that if we have made a mistake in translation of the English expression may not be -- for us should not be used. I apologise to the interpreters, for us, the English term cannot be used. Literally we meant "must not be used." For Sandian method, it says "may not be used," so we as engineers, we could take that with reservations that such a result would not have a high probability. With the Sandian laboratory method, it says clearly that when we apply it for light projectiles, then there are mistakes. This mistake could be to the highest 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake in what sense?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the calculated depth of the penetration of stabiliser. It would be 20 per cent would be maximum mistake. Then the coefficient of the form that is calculating. By comparing the examination results on ice. Specifically, Your Honours, let me explain.
