The Sandian laboratory is worked out for the needs of the federal government, and they've also measured the depth of penetration of projectiles in bombs of various projectiles for various grounds, for various surfaces. There was rock surface --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. My question was very simply: Do you maintain your conclusion that there isn't a shell that could reach this velocity at impact point so that it could become embedded in the surface, the stabiliser could get embedded? This is what the point of my question is:

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mortar -- a mortar projectile, 120-millimetre shell, there isn't a classical 120-millimetre mortar shell that could penetrate so deeply in such a type of surface, the way that it was presented that happened at Markale market, we used that as macadam.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What do you mean in classical 120-millimetre mortar? Are you trying to say that they could exist, that it does exist?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are other projectiles. There are active and reactive projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still 120?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, still 120. Yes, there is active and reactive 120-millimetre mortar shell with -- the very same. This is model 75 Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So -- so that I understand --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, this projectile, active reactive, does not have this type of stabiliser as was shown here. An active reactive 120-millimetre mortar shell of Yugoslav production which could have been found in that theatre of operations, in its structure is completely different from 120-millimetre mortar shell which is ordinary. It has a different stabiliser, tail fins open when the shell is fired, and the diameter is 3. So there are about 400 millimetres diameter. That's how much they -- their span is when they open but then it cannot be this stabiliser. This shell has higher velocity and higher impact velocity. That shell, not the stabiliser, but that shell could have hit or does hit -- hits the surface faster than standard classical 120-millimetre shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, in your report on page 52, and you mentioned that the two fragments where there is the B, what you are saying is there is a difference here, that these fragments do not belong to the same shell. You said something like that.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, asked by Mr. Stamp that we made some mistake, that when a shell explodes that there is a longer traces from the direction from where the shell has come compared to the one at the front trace. What I said was that this figure 313, only shows the parameters of the traces that are left in the surface from the -- from the fuse detonation in the frontal cosine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's page 52, but I'm speaking about the fragments.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fragments, the fragments on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where we can see B, there are two fragments marked "B."

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. As I said, 120-millimetre mortar shell has a thread, a filetage. This thread goes around the body of the shell so -- or has on top of the body of the shell so that we can have the fuse fitted in with a thread of 2 millimetres, but that would depend on the diameter of the fuse. When we have a light 120-millimetre shell, the thread to fit the stabiliser is 1.5 millimetres. It's a heavy shell. It's also 2 millimetres. The thread is 2 millimetres. On these pictures, in both cases the height --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what you're saying is that there is a difference. What I want to know simply is to be certain that I'm following you. Can you tell us what is the difference. Where is the difference between the two fragments? Because you're saying that the two fragments do not come from the same shell. Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This -- all this selection of fragments, so to speak, that were shown, in my assessment these fragments do not all belong to one projectile. Why not? Because when we have a mortar projectile, there are threads, the threads that are of 2 millimetres. And when we have a light shell, it's 1.5 millimetre, the thread. Here we have a thread which if this is 2 millimetres, that you can see these traces here, not just according to the thread but also according to the length of the coil of the thread in relation to the body of the shell. They do not correspond to the shell. They're not consistent with the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the two fragments marked "B," what you're saying is that they are -- what they're showing to be is that they do not come from the same shell. Is that what you're saying? Do you see a difference between these two except that one is larger than the other?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the size is concerned, these -- in these two fragments there's not much of a difference. However, these two fragments marked with "B," according to our assessment, they do belong to the same type of projectile but not mortar projectile. We assess that according to the length of the thread, it could be a rocket projectile. It could be a question of a rocket projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what can you tell by the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the photograph, roughly assessed they belong to the same projectile but they are not one in the same -- they do not belong to these other fragments. That is, there is a mix of fragments here. Unfortunately, we did ask the Defence and we were told that this was impossible to obtain, the proper result would be obtained if you did a mechanical and a graphical examination, analysis, of these fragments to find the exact structure of the fragments, to find out whether these fragments belonged to the same material belonging to the same projectile. This is just on the basis of geometry and the appearance of these fragments that we came to our conclusion. However, we came to a conclusion by comparing these fragments, or rather, this fragment with this fragment, and the thread which can be seen on these fragments, we've concluded that this cannot come -- originate from a mortar projectile because the mortar projectile doesn't have such a fine thread, such fine lines of its thread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, I don't want to take up too much time. You speak on page 41: [In English] "120-millimetres light mortar." [Interpretation] M-75. This is the third -- it's in the third paragraph from the bottom of the page. Yes. So what did you want to say by 120-millimetre light mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called it -- this mortar like this because we used the firing table for this mortar. That's what we used, used the firing tables for 120 mortar shell, model -- type M-75. This is official name, a light mortar 120-millimetre M-75, which according to the UNPROFOR report we saw, Your Honours, that these mortars were on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I understand correctly, M-75, this is to do with an artillery shell but not with a mortar. I mean, you have M-78. You have --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I apologise. This is a mortar shell-type M-75, so this was -- this is what it is -- no, it's not an artillery shell. It's a mortar shell. It's a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, it's a mortar shell --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a shell. It's a mortar of 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 120-millimetre mortar shell, yes, which uses a shell M-75, just that there are shells M-78.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. No, I'm sorry. 120-millimetre mortar M-75 can use a shell -- a mortar shell 120-millimetre model M -- P61. It can use different types of projectiles, from different years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any consequence? Why did you specify here that this was a light mortar M-75? Is there a difference, firing precision, force of firing? Is there any difference?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are differences between mortars. The weapons included four 120-millimetre shells. There was a Russian 120 millimetre, M-38 in the Yugoslav army. Then there was the universal mortar M-52 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But for the stabiliser that you saw, say that the stabiliser that was -- that was apparently found on the market, is that a stabiliser belonging to the light mortar or to some other mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a universal stabiliser which can be fitted on different types of shells, classical, typical -- when I say "classical," I mean of typical 120-millimetre mortar shells of Yugoslav manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To all shells.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for all types of manufacture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, I've got a few questions for you as well. Is my understanding correct that you use slightly different data, as far as 120-millimetre mortar shells are concerned if compared with the data given by Professor Zecevic? Perhaps you'd look at page 5 of your report. You give, for example, the --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, if I look at Professor Zecevic's report, he says, I think, that the explosive mass and type is 2.500 grams, whereas you take 2.250.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120-millimetre shell was made in the institute, and this is our official data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... stop me. I am just asking please listen carefully to my questions, Professor Vilicic. I'm asking you whether you and Dr. Zecevic are using different data in respect of these shells. Where they were made might be of interest to me, I'll then ask you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You studied the report of Dr. Zecevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you use different data, or do you not? For example, as far as the explosive mass or the shell case mass is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the professor knows less than the pupil, then enough said. We've used those results that we officially have in our documentation for projectiles that we made projects for, that we measured. If we have 2 kilos 500 for a heavy mortar shell, a 120-millimetre calibre, which has more explosive than a light mortar, a light mortar shell, that is listed here, has this average mass of explosive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you are using different data. I'm not asking for any explanation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an obvious difference in knowing the problem, in the knowledge of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be a possibility that shells were made in a different way under war circumstances or that shells were taken from somewhere else or -- I mean, what -- the easiest way of an expert to be not credible would be that he would use wrong data. That would be true for you and that would be true for Dr. Zecevic. Now, apart from that, you have explained to us that you are -- your knowledge seems to be superior to that of Dr. Zecevic. Do you have any other explanation for the difference in data?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me a question whether in wartime conditions, if there are circumstances to make a different projectile. Yes, it would have a thicker casing if it was not tasked, if it wasn't used according to standard terminology. It would have to be thicker casing so that there would be no premature explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, the shell case mass given by Dr. Zecevic is smaller, rather than bigger. Would you have any other explanation for the difference in data you are using and Dr. Zecevic is using?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not cast but forged.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Professor Stamatovic, Dr. Vukasinovic, and myself, we worked on making these projectiles. I have to say that Professor Zecevic never worked on 120-millimetre calibre shells. He was working with rocket technology, mostly with propellant for rockets, and that's why there are differences in his data and ours. These are official data that you can obtain and that you can see on documents for light high explosive 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say our figures are the official ones, so you have apart from that only that he might have made a mistake since he used to work in a different field. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked this. According to all the information that we have from 1958 to date, he didn't work on the mortar programme. He wasn't involved in that programme. Other people, unfortunately, are dead now, people from Sarajevo, they were involved in this project. They died before the war, after the war, not during the war, and we cooperated with them, we worked with them and carried out tests and so on and so on. I went to India with them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You confirmed what I asked you, I think, that I understood your answer well. May I take you to page 29 of your English version of the report. You write at the penultimate line: "If this doubt is justified, the shell had come from the north-eastern direction." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence, [In English] "Stationed in that direction either in the zone -- either in the zone between the territory under UNPROFOR controlled in Sarajevo airport or in the zone further to the north, controlled by Muslim ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- did you just find the place I just quoted to you in your report. You say "if this doubt is justified --"

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I then take you to your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shell had come from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this doubt is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I take you to your conclusion. And you say in your conclusion that without any -- it's page 33. You say "The firing position of the mortar that had fired the shell was situated at the range between three and four hundred metres in a north-eastern direction."

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the same shell of which you said that if the doubt would be justified, it would then have come from the north-eastern direction?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it concerns the same projectile. In fact, it concerns both projectiles. There were two projectiles which were fired at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And so in your report you say "If the doubt is justified, it would have come from the north-eastern direction." And in your final conclusion, you say, "It came from the north-eastern direction." If the doubt would not be justified, would it then have come from another direction?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We define that term in that manner because of the fact that the stabilisers weren't found. And on the basis of that fact, on the basis of the conclusions of the measurements in the field, we came to the assumption that the mortar shell in question was an 82-millimetre one. Having carried out a detailed analysis of this picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- The conclusion would remain the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I draw your attention to is that on page 29, you put a certain condition for the conclusion that the shell had come from the north-eastern direction, namely if the doubt you expressed was justified. I do not find a similar condition in your conclusion on page 33.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand you now. And there is a difference in -- as far as the terms are concerned. When it says "If doubt is justified," well, this phrase does not appear in the conclusion. We didn't include it in the conclusion. We said that after careful analysis of the ballistics evidence, this led to -- [In English] [Previous interpretation continues] ... if doubt is justified, we use other term, "lead to." In our language, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take you to page 31 of the English version of your report. You write the following: "Most probably firing position was at a distance of 300 to 400 metres. The range of 300 metres corresponds to the drop angle of 63 degrees. The range of 400 has a drop angle of 71 degrees." I have some difficulties in understanding this line because I took it from the other pictures used that a firing range of 300 metres, you would have a higher drop angle than at a firing range of 400 metres. Nevertheless, you give for 300 metres a drop angle of 63 per cent and for 400 metres, 71 per cent. Could you explain why here the smaller range would result in a smaller drop angle rather than in a higher drop angle?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the analysis on the basis of the depth of penetration, the depths of the craters which were measured on the site. So we came to the conclusion that the main charge was used. It has a 72-millimetre initial velocity. And on that basis, with no charges, if you fire at a range of 300 metres, the drop angle is 63 degrees. And if you fire at a range of 400 metres, the initial angle has to be greater in order to have a greater range. And then the drop angle - and I'm talking about the drop angle - is 71 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 71 is the steeper angle, isn't it? Shouldn't you in order to make a -- no, that's -- I'm afraid that I made a mistake. It's good that you explained to me that for a longer distance, that you need -- for the longer distance -- let me just -- if this is 63, would that bring a longer range than on 71? A steeper firing angle, would that produce a shorter trajectory, as far as distance is concerned, or would it result in a longer trajectory as far as distance is concerned? I'll just ask you --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the drop angles. The drop angle is greater, the greater the range is. So with the main charge you have a drop angle -- if the firing angle is 45 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the drop angle, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat -- but perhaps I'll stop you for one second. Could I please ask you --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest range is obtained if you have a firing angle of 45 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- could you please look at this small sketch. And before doing so, may I ask you that -- whether a higher firing angle produces a higher drop angle or is there any misunderstanding on my side?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please explain to me --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a higher firing angle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, produces a high drop --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Produces a high drop angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you now please look at this, without changing it. I have tried to sketch approximately a 70 degree firing angle, and I assumed that that would result also in a higher drop angle. And I have done this same for a lower firing angle. And I have some difficulties in understanding that with the higher angle you get the longer distance, the longer trajectory. But perhaps I've taken the angles wrong or -- could you explain why you come to the conclusion that a drop angle of 63 degrees would correspond with a short trajectory and why a 60 per cent -- a 60 degrees drop angle would correspond with the longer distance. Could you please -- could you please try to tell me what is wrong in my understanding as it appears in this small sketch I made, because in the small sketch the 70 degree, the steeper angle, produces a shorter distance; whereas, in your report, it's just the opposite, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please explain me what is wrong in my understanding, or did you make a mistake here on the ...?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't have the firing table here, but I have to say that if you have a higher angle, a higher firing angle, the ranges are greater. When you drew this diagram, you assumed that the trajectories were more or less the same, but there are greater differences. I have to say that I can't answer your question precisely. I agree with you that the drop angle is greater, that if you have a greater firing angle, the drop angle is greater. But it seems that a smaller distance corresponds to a greater drop angle and a greater distance to a smaller drop angle. Obviously there is a mistake here. But in order to be 100 per cent precise and to confirm this - I don't have a firing table here - and 71 and 63 are angles which according to this -- these graphic tables that I have here, they would correspond to the main charge, to the basic charge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness mentioned that the peak of the trajectory is not being the same.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A greater drop angle corresponds to a smaller range. Your conclusion is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the conclusion in your report is not --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake. These numbers were changed. Instead of 300 metres -- I can see 300 metres here in the tables. That would correspond to an angle between 65 -- 60 and 65 degrees, and 470 metres would correspond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to see whether I understood your report well, and I see that here perhaps the figures might have been interchanged. It's not of great relevance at this very moment to see exactly what it is. May I ask your attention for the following part of your report. May I take you to page 46. If I take you to page 46. Approximately in the middle of the page you say, "If at the distance of about 100 metres from this locality barracks of Muslim forces are situated, it is possible that they were the target to weapons located in different positions at different ranges from the barracks." What is the basis -- the factual basis of this observation you make? You see, if at a distance of --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you take it for your opinion as relevant? What is the source of Muslim forces' barracks at a distance of about 100 metres?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We came to this conclusion because of the fact that the firing between the first and second projectile, the interval was between two and three minutes. And on the other hand, the magnitude of the dispersion, if the same elements had been used to fire, the dispersion would not have been as significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again and ask you again to listen carefully to my question. My question was: On the basis of what did you make an assumption here of the presence of barracks of Muslim forces at a distance of about 100 metres? That's the only thing. Did someone tell you? Did you read it somewhere? Are you personally aware of -- what is the basis of knowledge of this fact?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witness number 1, mentioned in the report on page 44, he said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just, if you say that you have --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw this in his statement and we mentioned this here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since statement number 1, the material that was provided to us by the Defence, in the records that we were given which contained witness statements, the witness Zahida Kadric stated this, and we linked this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I'm interested in: You say the source is the statement of Mr. Kadric. That's what I'd like to know. Then could I take you to page -- now, first of all, perhaps, I'll take you to a question put by -- I think by Judge Nieto-Navia, who asked you whether on the basis of methodology you would agree with Professor Zecevic. And you explained that you did not agree, and one of the reasons you gave is that Professor Zecevic would have said that 60 metres per second would not be sufficient for a projectile to penetrate into the ground. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Professor Zecevic said that 60 metres was a speed which was sufficient for the ground to be penetrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have at least this to be -- this clarified, because in the transcript it reads different. So you say because he said that the penetration of, I think, 25 centimetres was possible at a speed of 30 metres per second, you disagree with that and you would -- in your opinion, you would require a higher speed.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that it was 60 metres, give or take 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 10 per cent, or 10 metres. Apart from that, is there any other -- because this is perhaps not a methodological difference between you and Professor Zecevic but, rather, the tables or the coefficients you used that distinguishes your opinions. Is there any fundamental difference of view in respect of speed of arrival of the projectile compensating the back-pushing power of the detonation and then remaining sufficient speed to embed into the ground? I see quite some similarity in your methodology and the methodology of Professor Zecevic, apart from the difference in outcome. Is this perception correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we stated that the most complete analysis in technical terms was carried out for the Markale case, and Professor Zecevic participated in this. This was the report on the massacre at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, I'm just asking you whether the basics of your methodology, if you compare it with the one of Dr. Zecevic, whether the basis of your methodology is the same.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, yes. But not with regard to all issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. There are differences. That also explains why you come to different conclusions. My next question is: You made a calculation of the Markale market -- but perhaps I would -- I have three more questions for you. Perhaps I'll leave them for after the break, because tapes -- we are running out of tapes and we'll not be able to finish in two or three minutes. We'll adjourn until 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Vilicic, may I take you to page 53 of your report, English version. You are writing, "If the expression for theta C is used to calculate elliptical impressions ..." Have you found that part? Could you explain to me what these four lines exactly are about, because my problem in understanding is the following: You say "if the expression for theta C is used to calculate elliptical impressions on the ground --" I take it on the ground, "recorded at Markale market after explosion of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. calibre 120-millimetre mortar shell." And then you say, "A is 56, B is 26, and theta C is 41 degrees." What I do not understand is you say that you are calculating something where theta C is known or unknown, it's not quite clear, whereas theta C is given as 41 degrees, and then you say for the first increment charge theta C is 65 and for the sixth increment charge theta C is 56. I have some difficulties in understanding what exactly you are calculating on the basis of what? Or is it your view that it's not well written down in English and could therefore create confusion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- just a moment. Let me have a look. What I mean is that is true, yes, considering the drop angle. To determine a drop angle, you take the starting point as being that with the first increment, if the shell landed by calculations that there was an angle of 41 degrees, it would be consistent with the projectile fired with the first increment charge and then with the sixth increment charge, because as you know, the size of the image -- of the impression would depend on the drop angle if it went down with the first increment charge, then the coordinates of the elliptical form 56 and 26, that would correspond to the 41 degree angle. And if it was fired with a sixth increment charge, then these coordinates, 56 and 26, would be corresponding to a drop angle of 62.5 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Should I then read these lines as follows, that if you want to deduce from the elliptical impressions on the ground recorded at Markale market after explosion of a calibre 120-millimetre mortar shell which gives A as 56 and B as 26, that on a first increment, that would mean that the drop angle would have been 41 degrees and that for the first increment charge it would be 62 degrees and for the sixth increment charge --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- It would be 55.6? Is that the right understanding?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, that's correct. Just like what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you now explain that if the increment charges are increasing, if I do understand you correctly -- although, in your testimony you just said that 41 degrees corresponded with the first increment charge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I said it was 41 degrees is corresponding to the first increment charge? I don't think so. I don't think that's what I said. The first increment charge is corresponding to the angle of 62.5 degrees, while the sixth increment charge would be of a lower angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you said is --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a mistake. Could you then please --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now. The first increment charge for the impression with values 56 and 26, the semi-axis of the elliptical form, and the frontal swathe of the shell dispersion, the first increment charge is corresponding to the 62.5 degrees, and the sixth increment would be corresponding to 55.6 degrees. That's what should be in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand. And you made most of your calculations on the basis of 55.6 degree drop angle; is that correct? Very often you used this figure of 55.6, which also corresponds with your -- yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the drop angle which corresponds to the longest range and to the highest impact velocity for the lower category of angles. 86.2 degrees, that is the maximum range of -- or maximum category of angles. These are the two values, corresponding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I could not follow. Where is the mistake? Because you repeated the same figures.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The mistake was that it was written that I said for the first increment charge the angle was 41 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The mistake is in the transcript, not in your report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you please. Pay attention to the figure 313. Theta 1 is the angle that is formed by the triangle OCB. That is theta 1 angle. Theta 1 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I understand. In the transcript, not to your report.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Theta 1 is 41 degrees. That corresponds to theta 1. That is corresponding to the triangle, the axis of the projectile that forms the triangle with the back part. That is OCB triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you did, as a matter of fact, is you mentioned theta C to be 41 degrees where you intended to say that it was theta 1.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theta 1 is 41 degrees. And for theta 1 being 41 degrees, that's what you get the angle of being 62.5, that is 55.6 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Because the report says "theta C, 41." So that's a mistake in the report. Let me just see whether I have -- yes. I have --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theta 1? I'm sorry, theta 1, it says also in the report, it says theta 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But on your -- in the middle of the line I just read to you, that says theta C.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can have a look. [In English] Oh, yes. Mistakes. Serbian, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That happens. Yes. You made a calculation for the hit probability for the Markale market and you said that the dimension of the target was 36 by 30 metres. Am I right in understanding that you limited your calculation to the marketplace itself without the adjacent street to be included, so not the whole open area but just a limited part of it? If you look at page 48 of your report, I find an open space which seems to be measured as 41 metres by 35 metres, page 48. And now, I do include the street as part of an open space. Is my understanding correct that -- I do not know exactly what figures you used, because 36 by 30 does not appear.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance from this building, which is 3.65 metres tall, up to the street in Markale, the distance is 30 metres from that point. And the width of the street was taken to be roughly 5 metres. That's why it says "35 metres" here. We didn't have the exact dimensions for this area. So for an area of 30 times 35 -- 30 by 35, we assumed that there was one person on each square metre, in other words, that there were 1.152 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- how people would be hit by the -- the total area, do you agree with me that the total area --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... would be approximately one-third, if you express it in the surface?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we had used the dimensions provided on the sketch, the area would be even greater and there would have been even more people in that area, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A greater area, would that mean easier to hit and more people there as potential people to be injured or ...?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we take the figure 40 by 30, there would have been 1.200 people. We took the dimensions 30 by 35, and that was 1152 people. We eliminated a surface of 250 square centimetres, so there were no obstacles that would have protected those people who were there in Markale, those metal stalls, we eliminated that in order to obtain the maximum number of people hit. Secondly, we didn't take into consideration the fact that when one person is hit by a fragment, energy is lost and the person in the vicinity is not wounded or is only lightly wounded. We assumed that the fragment did not encounter any kind of resistance, in other words, that the resistance -- we assumed that the resistance provided by the people who were there was zero. The fragments were assumed to be able to continue their trajectory without encountering obstacles of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course a resistance of zero is unrealistic. In fact, it is presumed to have been higher?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's impossible. Because the lethal energy is 100 jules. So any fragment that hits someone with such energy it loses energy when inflicting a wound as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are my questions for you, Professor Vilicic. Are there any questions arising from the questions of the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't know if the Prosecution also has questions to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware that the Chamber took a lot of time. Nevertheless, I would like the parties to try to be as concise as possible. And I'm inviting you as well, Professor Vilicic, to give as precise answers as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly. We'll just follow your example, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in regards to a question put to you by Judge El Mahdi, you spoke about two types of mortars -- mortar shells, 120-millimetre light mortar and 120-millimetre heavy mortar. Could you briefly tell us what the difference is between the two types of these mortar shells is. And secondly, if I have understood you correctly, could you tell us why it is not possible to confuse these two types in relation to the Markale incident or in relation to the other incidents?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there can be no confusion in our analysis because we took the least favourable mortar. A light mortar has an initial velocity of 322 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'll stop you there. But what's the difference between a heavy 120-millimetre mortar and a light 120-millimetre mortar? The Defence is not quite clear about this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only difference is in the total mass of those mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that 120-millimetre M-75 mortar was the most modern mortar type and it can fire with a greater charge, it can have a greater weight, and then the shell can have a greater initial speed when fired. Its initial speed is 322 metres, whereas an M-38 mortar can't -- it can't be fired from because there are certain obstacles with regard to the maximum pressure that the barrel of the mortar can put up with. So you can only use a maximum of five charges for such mortars, and this includes using new shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to return to the subject of 120-millimetre assisted mortars, what we call assisted mortars. You said that on the basis of the stabiliser you could make a distinction. My question is as follows: In what respects are these stabilisers different? How is it possible to avoid confusing the two types of stabilisers?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the appearance. These stabilisers with an active reactive projectile, the stabiliser, when it comes out of the barrel it opens its fins, so it has fins over the calibres. When the fins open up, then the diameter of the fins is greater. There are four fins. It has four fins, whereas, the other mortar has a fixed stabiliser and the stabiliser is the same as that of the shell, 120 millimetres. But in this case, it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'd like to take you back to what you mentioned on page 42 of your report. I'm talking about the English version -- on page 52 of your report. Do you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at fragment B, in the upper part. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you wanted to say something in relation to the length of this fragment and in relation to the thread, I think, but your answer wasn't complete. What did you want to say at that point?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the body of a mortar shell has engraved grooves for the fuse and the diameter is 2 millimetres. So if B has a 2-millimetre diameter, then the other fragments that you can see -- well, you can see certain grooves -- these fragments don't correspond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regard to this matter, you said that there was a mixture involved here. And I think that you added other information. I think that you said something with regard to the origin itself of these fragments. Could you please provide this additional information. At the time, I was listening to the Serbian channel, that's why I'm drawing your attention to this now.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the fragments marked by the letter "B" at the top of the figure and down below - and the Judge asked me about this - I said that these fragments belonged to the same type of projectile, given the grooves that you can see on them. If you want me to continue commenting on this -- well, if this belongs to a projectile, but our conclusion was that it isn't -- it wasn't part of one projectile, it didn't belong to one projectile -- these are facts noted by the expert Higgs too. The colour of the material is different. The two semicircular fragments were designated as parts of the shell's reductor by the expert Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, you said that that didn't form part of one projectile. I think that that's what I heard when listening to the Serbian booth. But did you mean to say that it formed part -- that it belonged to several projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we came to this conclusion, we didn't have information from UNPROFOR's report in which it is stated that the official representative of BH, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, gave up the evidence on these fragments. He didn't take this into consideration because he -- he decided to say that they didn't belong to the same projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question, Professor: Since you said that these photographs represented fragments which according to your testimony belonged to several projectiles, what do you deduce from this scientifically speaking?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we came to the conclusion that in order to assert that this belonged to one projectile, it would be necessary to carry out a mechanical examination and it wasn't possible to do this because the Defence team said that these samples weren't available. And after this conclusion - that's why we didn't change it later on - Mr. Jamakovic agreed. It's page 303, 8409 of the UNPROFOR report. Mr. Jamakovic agreed to provide us with the fins taken from the crater and to provide the team with shrapnel, which was apparently taken from the market. Since they were not in a position to prove that it was really shrapnel from the 5th of February explosion, they agreed that this would not be of much assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, it is three minutes past 7.00. If you would have a number of questions, we should adjourn until tomorrow. If there would be only one, two, or three questions, then we could ask the interpreters and the technicians whether we could finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Three questions, three or four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just proceed quickly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, could we finish today as far as the interpreters and the technicians are concerned? And of course the registry also has to verify whether the transportation of -- are the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not a problem for the interpreters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you again for your great flexibility. And if you proceed quickly, Mr. Stamp, and if you, Professor Vilicic, give precise answers, then we might finish within a couple of minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in answer to a question by His Honour Judge Nieto-Navia that all your calculations show that it is not possible for the stabiliser fin to penetrate as far as Professor Zecevic saw it. And further in answer to His Honour El Mahdi, you said "taking into account --" you said that you did your analysis taking into account the layer of 2 centimetres asphalt. I wish to suggest to you, sir, that --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, no. I didn't say that we use in account 2 centimetres of asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked a question in relation to an upper layer of concrete or asphalt and you took that into account. I would like to suggest to you that if one applies the Berezansky formula, using the same values that you used in the table that you presented entitled "Impact velocity VP of the stabiliser of a mortar shell 120-millimetre for penetration LP in various targets theta 0 equals 65.6 degrees," the results obtained on a proper application of that formula to the values in these tables would be different from the ones that you have presented to the Court in these tables. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't just agree with such a statement without precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I suggest to you that if one applies the Berezansky formula to the same values that you have in the first column, then the penetration or the results in respect of the depth of penetration would be higher than what you have presented to the Court. And I suggest to you the same would be true if you applied the other formulas, the Panka [phoen] formula and the Petry [phoen] formula, that all of them would result in higher levels of penetration. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which other methods? If computers are coming up with the wrong results, then we came up with the wrong results too. You have the calculators here which were done with a -- with a Mac, these are the values obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Therefore, you disagree with my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree that we had taken 2 centimetres of asphalt into consideration, into account. I never say that. I said the asphalt could be even harder than concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... is that you had misapplied the Berezansky formula and the results presented in the table for depth of penetration are not correct for the various impact velocities. Do you disagree or agree? Please, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I don't agree with you at all. That would mean that we're not able to do mathematical calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Second question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fourth question, Mr. Stamp. As a matter of fact, I do understand that perhaps from your common law background that you find this do you agree, do you disagree absolutely necessary. It does not add much to the testimony given until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's really try to finish now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the same answers which you gave, I suggest to you that in respect to the Markale incident, the mortar round exploded on contact and therefore the tail fin did not penetrate the asphalt as the explosion, the blast of the explosion, had created a 9-centimetre deep crater before the stabiliser continued into the ground and therefore the only surface to measure in respect to stabiliser penetration was the soil beneath the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Professor Vilicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading the transcript because in the translation some surface that was penetrated was mentioned. That doesn't appear anywhere. That has to do with the surface of the diameter of the projectile, according to the Berezansky formula, cross-section. [In English] It is written that only surface to measure in respect to stabiliser penetration was the soil beneath the asphalt. Maybe it's material in question you'd like to say, material in question after --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, material in question after the surface has been blasted away to create the crater. The material was soil.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the explosion would only have made a hole, a crater, no. For there to be an explosion without the projectile to become embedded, no, it couldn't create a 9-centimetre deep crater. That sort of a crater can be made been an explosive device but not by a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And lastly, in answer to a question from the President of the Chamber, you said that your analysis was on the basis of the depth of penetration, the depth of the crater's. And that is your analysis that you have made in your report at section 2.4, and you have used the tables 7 and 8. I suggest to you that that entire section of your report and those tables do not apply to fuses or to rounds with fuses set to impact on contact. That is a modern impact fuses of super quick action which are tested to activate before they penetrate 24.5 millimetres. It relates to slower fuses, and therefore all your conclusions in respect to impact velocity, drop angles, range, which precedes from section 2.4, do not apply to faster impact fuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question doesn't seem to arise from the questions put to the witness by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it greatly assists or not. But Professor Vilicic, could you just say whether you would agree or if you would not agree with what just has been suggested to you by Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree because the mechanics would all come to nothing. Mechanics would all come to nothing in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And to the Court, I have copies of all statements of Derida Tadic [phoen] and if the Court so pleases we can show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But as such, these statements are not in evidence. And I think it's quite clear that the Defence has presented material that was not in evidence, and the Chamber I think earlier has made clear that an expert witness is not an instrument through which you introduce new evidence that has not been subject to cross-examination by the other party. So the Chamber as such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the Chamber does not seek this evidence to be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Although, may I just indicate that what we would have sought to show is separate and apart from the issue of whether she testified or not but what she said in her statement and whether or not there would have been a basis for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not alter its position in respect of seeking access to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That will be all, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Vilicic, it has been a couple of very long days for you, and it's certainly asked the utmost of your concentration. We thank you very much for having come to The Hague and to testify in this court. It was not the first time that we saw you, so you travelled several times, and that's -- of course the most important thing is you answered the questions of both parties and the questions of the Judges. You even now and then gave more than answers to the questions of the parties and the Judges. We thank you very much for having come to testify in this court, and we wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was an honour for me to present our results, our analysis. I'll only take a minute. You said that I would be able to address you at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I would be able to say a few things. Could I just say this: With regard to Mr. Stamp's claim that an 82-millimetre mortar shell, that its stabiliser never remains on the site, I'd like to say that the calculations show and practice also bears this out, that with a projectile that has 50 per cent of TNT and hexogen substance, the ejection speed is 158 metres and if it just has TNT, it's 148 metres. So with the main charge, the stabiliser is always in the vicinity of the point of impact of the projectile. Thank you, and I apologise for taking up additional minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a bit of a problem, Professor Vilicic, because you as a matter of fact gave additional information without being asked about it. Mr. Stamp, is it really necessary to give you an opportunity to -- if you say no, I'll not do it. If you say no -- because it's an issue you raised, and now unexpectedly the witness comes up. So if it's something you'd like to deal with, then I think I should allow you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is something I'd like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then do that extremely briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if that could be dealt with within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not within half an hour. Then I would say that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You caused us a little problem, Professor Vilicic. No, I do understand that you're a technical expert and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. But yesterday such a categorical claim that we were not right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... yes. The matter is that yesterday we stopped that. Now you raised the issue again, and therefore the Chamber considers that although we have not sought this, that Mr. Stamp should be able to put additional questions. If -- are you still available tomorrow early in the afternoon for, let's say, 15 minutes, 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my plane is tomorrow morning for Belgrade, 10.40 or 10.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case I could be very short. I'll just put the position to him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then he may agree or not agree. Let's keep it to that. Otherwise, another solution would be that we just say that this is not evidence but a remark made by the witness, because we can't just continue for -- if it just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put your position to the witness, then see whether he agrees or disagrees so that it has been put from your side, and then -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will accept this, Mr. President, hoping this will be of exemplary decision, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware that the Chamber is not happy to choose this path at this very moment, but to keep the witness for another day would perhaps be too much. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, Professor, is it correct that the weapons -- that the ejection of the stabiliser fin by Dr. Vukasinovic et al., is based on the Duval formula, that is, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter in the Serbian booth did not hear the name of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the detachment velocity, that is, the velocity that push back the 82-millimetre stabiliser by all standard recognised tests is much faster than any possible approach speed of the 82-millimetre round.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which shell? Whose shell? Whose manufacture shell would that be? A Yugoslav shell has a steel stabiliser and weight of 400 grams. You can make the calculation and find out that it is impossible for it to have a velocity higher than the drop velocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question was whether the detonation effect of an exploding 82-millimetre mortar shell, detonation effect that would push backwards the tail fin, would be such that the tail fin will always be stopped and will never penetrate into the ground because its speed of impact will be too low to overcome that detonation effect. Do you agree with that or do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that the stabiliser of an 82-millimetre shell will not penetrate the surface, the ground. The only question was whether the push-back velocity is higher than the drop velocity. We are saying that it is not higher than the drop velocity of the highest increments, third or fourth increment charges of an 82-millimetre shell, which is why the stabiliser remains close to the impact site. At the football match you saw that the stabilisers were not found because they were pushed back, they were rejected, because the velocity of the projectile wasn't very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that there are aluminium stabilisers for the 82-millimetre weighing 0.165 [Realtime transcript read in error "0.65"] grams and there are stabilisers weighing 0.45 grams. Are you aware that there are aluminium stabilisers for the 82-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are such things as aluminium stabilisers, and the calculation I gave you was for an aluminium stabiliser. But not here. Here in the text it's wrong, that it is only 0.61 grams and 0.45. No, that's probably wrong. It's 0.61 pounds and 0.45 pounds, not grams. Because that's 250 to 200 grams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you do not have any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The metric system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said pounds, instead of grams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have -- not below a gram, below a kilogramme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are far below a gram. And I think the witness rectified that where you said 0.61 grams, that it should be 0.61 pounds, and that is still far under 1 kilogramme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The figures are 0.165 kilogrammes and 0.450 kilogrammes for the steel stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be correct, Professor Vilicic? Same figures but then kilogrammes rather than pounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other way around. Your Honours, if we're speak about the steel stabiliser, it can be 610 grams. And if it's aluminium, 450 grams. Stabilisers that are heavier than 400 grams regularly remain or, that is, they have such energy and such impulse that with higher charges will remain at the site of the impact. If they are less than 400 grams, it would fly back, you would never find it on the site of the impact. That's why I've asked you whose shell. Yugoslav shells have these stabilisers, heavier than 400 grams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that the matter has been sufficiently clarified. Is there any additional questions? No further questions. Then Professor Vilicic, I'll make it very brief to you. I'll repeat whatever I said ten minutes ago to you. I wish you a safe trip home again. We'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.29 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of March, 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
